query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation and catastrophic failure of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy during high-temperature exposure are governed by a threshold reactive gas composition that promotes rapid, localized oxidation (or reduction) along grain boundaries enriched by additive manufacturing–induced segregation and residual stresses. This localized reaction forms brittle intergranular oxide (or reduced) layers that precipitate catastrophic mechanical failure.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured alloy with a face‐centered cubic (fcc) matrix exhibiting non-equilibrium microstructures, residual stresses, and potential elemental segregation along grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the oxygen partial pressure (and corresponding hydrogen/reducing gas fraction) during high-temperature exposures.
generation.conditions: Exposures performed at 700–1100°C under controlled atmospheres, comparing lower reactive gas compositions (baseline) versus higher oxygen (or reducing gas) partial pressures.
generation.structural_mediator: Localized grain boundary oxidation/reduction promoted by segregated elements and residual stresses, leading to the formation of brittle intergranular phases.
generation.mechanism: When the reactive gas composition exceeds a critical threshold, the locally enriched grain boundaries rapidly undergo oxidation (or reduction), forming brittle phases that weaken intergranular cohesion. The intricate additive manufacturing–induced microstructure thus predisposes the alloy to intergranular crack initiation and subsequent catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to higher oxygen (or reducing gas) partial pressures will exhibit earlier onset of intergranular oxide (or reduced phase) formation, detectable via in situ monitoring techniques (e.g., acoustic emission or real-time microscopy), and will fail catastrophically sooner compared to baseline samples exposed at lower reactive gas levels.
generation.baseline: The initial additively manufactured material exposed to lower reactive gas compositions shows slower oxidation/reduction kinetics, fewer brittle intergranular features, and no rapid catastrophic failure within the same exposure timescale.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies within the elevated temperature range of 700–1100°C under atmospheres where the oxygen (or hydrogen) partial pressure can be precisely controlled. The hypothesis is most relevant when the testing duration is sufficient to allow intergranular chemical reactions to develop (ranging from hours to hundreds of hours).
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold value of reactive gas partial pressure that triggers the rapid localized oxidation or reduction, as well as the detailed kinetics of the intergranular phase formation, remain uncertain due to variations in microstructural heterogeneity inherent to additive manufacturing processes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy samples and subject them to high-temperature exposures (700–1100°C) under atmospheres with systematically varied oxygen partial pressures (and matched reducing gas compositions). Use in situ monitoring (e.g., acoustic emission sensors and real-time microscopy) to detect the onset of intergranular oxidation/reduction. Follow the exposures with mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or creep tests) and post-mortem microstructural characterization (e.g., EDS, XRD) to identify brittle intergranular phases.
measurements: Time-to-onset of acoustic emissions indicating intergranular cracking
Real-time imaging data capturing oxidation/reduction at grain boundaries
Mechanical strength and failure mode from tensile/creep tests
Chemical and phase analysis of grain boundaries via EDS and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the oxygen (or reducing gas) partial pressure does not result in an earlier onset of localized intergranular oxidation/reduction or does not correlate with earlier catastrophic failure compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In summary, our study deciphers an unusual ductile−brittle−ductile transition in a eutectic HEA, driven by the dynamic evolution of LCOs and PBs configurations. Enhanced LCOs and the formation of jagged PBs lead to brittleness, while controlling the order degree of LCOs and the formation of a ductile transition zone along the PBs recovers the ductility. This discovery highlights the critical role of nanoscale chemical heterogeneities and PBs in determining material behavior, challenging and expanding the traditional paradigm of thermal embrittlement. Although LCOs are generally beneficial for strength‐ductility synergy in HEAs, our findings reveal their dual role: excessive ordering induces brittleness, whereas controlled LCOs restore ductility, which further indicates the necessity of meticulous control of LCOs for better performance. We believe that the uncover of thermal evolution behavior of HEA will advance the high‐temperature application of the HEA family.

Abstract Oxidation behavior of a refractory AlNbTiVZr 0.25 high-entropy alloy at 600–900 °C was investigated. At 600–700 °C, two-stage oxidation kinetics was found: Nearly parabolic oxidation (n = 0.46–0.48) at the first stage, transitioned to breakaway oxidation (n = 0.75–0.72) at the second stage. At 800 °C, the oxidation kinetics was nearly linear (n = 0.92) throughout the entire duration of testing. At 900 °C, the specimen disintegrated after 50 h of testing. The specific mass gains were estimated to be 7.2, 38.1, and 107.5, and 225.5 mg/cm 2 at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h, and 900 °C for 50 h, respectively. Phase compositions and morphology of the oxide scales were analyzed using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). It was shown that the surface layer at 600 °C consisted of the V 2 O 5 , VO 2 , TiO 2 , Nb 2 O 5 , and TiNb 2 O 7 oxides. Meanwhile, the scale at 900 °C comprised of complex TiNb 2 O 7 , AlNbO 4 , and Nb 2 Zr 6 O 17 oxides. The oxidation mechanisms operating at different temperatures were discussed and a comparison of oxidation characteristics with the other alloys was conducted. frame.system: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a face‐centered cubic (fcc) matrix, which inherently exhibits additive manufacturing features such as residual stresses, non-equilibrium microstructures, and possible segregation at grain boundaries.
frame.goal: Uncover and validate the mechanistic link between elevated-temperature exposure in reactive (oxidizing or reducing) atmospheres and the onset of degradation leading to catastrophic failure.
frame.limitation: The current understanding does not clearly define how interactions at the microstructural level—such as diffusion, oxidation kinetics, and phase transformations—under high-temperature gas exposures translate into rapid, catastrophic failure, nor is there a controlled experiment that isolates these factors.
constraints: Hypothesis must be testable with controlled experimental perturbations

Make clear, baseline-referenced predictions in observations
Define applicable exposure boundaries (e.g., temperature ranges and gas compositions)

Establish a clear falsification criterion for the hypothesis
frame.regime: Elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., 700–1100°C) under controlled atmospheres, where one set of experiments uses an oxidizing environment (high oxygen partial pressure) and another uses a reducing gas (e.g., hydrogen-containing atmosphere). Temperature, gas composition, and ramp rates should be tightly regulated.
prior_attempts: Prior studies on similar high-entropy alloys or conventional alloys have primarily tracked weight change, oxide scale formation, or microstructural evolution via post-mortem analyses, but lacked systematic, controlled changes to correlate gas composition effects with mechanical failure modes.
Earlier experiments did not fully isolate the role of additive manufacturing–induced microstructural heterogeneities on the oxidation/reduction kinetics under high-temperature exposure.

decision.trend: Early work in HEAs has largely characterized high‐temperature degradation by post‐mortem measurements – for example, tracking weight changes and oxide scale formation in refractory systems (PMC5578249) or identifying tempering‐like embrittlement through phase boundary evolution in Al-containing alloys (PMC12806431). These studies showed that microstructural features such as grain boundary segregation and secondary phase formation can lead to brittle, intergranular fracture. However, none of these efforts isolated how the varying gas composition (oxidizing vs. reducing environments) interacts with the unique non-equilibrium microstructures intrinsic to additive manufacturing. Thus, while oxidation or reduction kinetics and amorphous intergranular layer formation have been observed, the specific threshold conditions under which these interactions yield catastrophic failure remain unclarified.
decision.unsolved: It remains unsolved how the additive manufacturing–specific microstructural heterogeneities (e.g., residual stresses, segregation at grain boundaries, and non-equilibrium phase distributions) modulate oxidation/reduction kinetics under high-temperature gas exposure. In particular, the critical role of the reactive gas composition – the oxygen (or hydrogen) partial pressure that triggers localized, rapid oxidation (or reduction) at these vulnerable microstructural sites leading to catastrophic rupture – has not been pinpointed.
decision.lever: systematically vary the oxygen partial pressure (and by extension the reducing gas fraction) during exposures at 700–1100°C while employing in situ monitoring techniques (e.g., acoustic emission or real-time microscopy) to capture the onset of intergranular oxidation/reduction and correlated mechanical degradation.
decision.why: Controlling the reactive gas composition directly targets the suspected mechanism – that additive manufacturing-induced grain boundary segregations and residual stresses predispose the alloy to rapid, localized oxidation or reduction. By mapping the degradation behavior against finely tuned gas compositions and controlled thermal conditions, this experiment would clearly test the hypothesis that a threshold oxygen (or hydrogen) partial pressure governs catastrophic failure. This step logically follows the trend of previous studies that documented oxidation kinetics and embrittlement, while filling the gap of directly linking gas composition to the failure mode.
